kydonia.t: Leading city of western Crete for much of antiquity, a rival of Knossos and Gortyn, on the site of modern Chania.
kydonia.o: Kydonia stood on a Minoan site on the north-west coast of Crete. Herodotus records that Samian exiles fleeing Polycrates settled there in 524 BCE and built temples, before Aeginetans defeated them in 519 BCE and settled the city in their turn. By the classical period it was an independent Cretan polis named after its legendary founder Kydon.
kydonia.r: Kydonia was governed, like other Cretan cities, by annual officials called kosmoi and a council of elders, with a warrior aristocracy and dependent rural labourers. It struck silver coins, traded across the Aegean and supplied mercenaries, including famous archers. In the Hellenistic period it fought repeated wars with Knossos, Gortyn and Polyrrhenia.
kydonia.e: Rome intervened in Crete during the wars against the Cretan pirates. Quintus Caecilius Metellus besieged and took Kydonia in 69 BCE on his way to conquering the island, which became part of the province of Crete and Cyrene. Kydonia remained a free city under Rome and survives as Chania.

kingdom-of-amathus.t: Cypriot kingdom on the south coast that kept the island's pre-Greek Eteocypriot language alive into the 4th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.o: Amathus was founded c. 1050 BCE on a hill near modern Limassol. Ancient writers regarded its people as autochthonous Cypriots, and the city preserved the Eteocypriot language, written in the Cypriot syllabary, alongside Greek. It also had close links with Phoenicia, and its rulers paid tribute to Assyria in the 7th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.r: The acropolis held a palace and a major sanctuary of the Cypriot goddess later called Aphrodite, with a giant stone vase now in the Louvre. The kingdom grew rich from copper and agriculture. It was loyal to Persia: in 498 BCE it refused to join the revolt led by Onesilus of Salamis and was besieged.
kingdom-of-amathus.e: King Androcles sent ships to help Alexander the Great at Tyre in 332 BCE. The monarchy was ended under Ptolemy I c. 312 BCE, and Amathus continued as a city under the Ptolemaic Empire and Rome. It declined after the 7th century CE and was abandoned.

kingdom-of-sussex.t: The kingdom of the South Saxons on the English Channel coast, among the earliest Anglo-Saxon realms and the last major one to accept Christianity.
kingdom-of-sussex.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says that Aelle and his three sons landed in 477 and fought the Britons near the shore, later storming the Roman fort of Anderitum (Pevensey) in 491. Bede names Aelle as the first overlord of the southern English. Settlement was hemmed in by the dense Weald forest, which isolated the kingdom from its neighbours.
kingdom-of-sussex.r: Sussex was small and inward-looking, with a farming economy on the coastal plain and the chalk downs. Its kings often stood under Mercian or West Saxon overlordship. Paganism lasted until Wilfrid of York converted the South Saxons in the 680s, founding a monastery and bishopric at Selsey on land given by King Aethelwealh. Several kings sometimes ruled at once.
kingdom-of-sussex.e: Caedwalla of Wessex overran Sussex in the 680s, and in the 8th century it fell under Offa of Mercia. After Ecgberht's victory at Ellendun in 825, Sussex submitted to the Kingdom of Wessex and became a shire. The name survives in the modern counties of East and West Sussex.

kingdom-of-aragon.t: The Pyrenean kingdom that conquered the Ebro valley, joined Catalonia to form the Crown of Aragon and kept its own laws until 1707.
kingdom-of-aragon.o: Aragon began as a small Carolingian-era county around Jaca. In 1035 Sancho III of Navarre left it to his son Ramiro I, who ruled as king in practice. His heirs Sancho Ramírez and Peter I expanded south, taking Huesca in 1096, and Alfonso I the Battler captured Zaragoza in 1118.
kingdom-of-aragon.r: The kingdom developed strong traditions of noble privilege: its Cortes, its fueros and the Justicia de Aragón, a judge who guarded the laws even against the king. Its economy rested on Ebro valley farming, wool and the many Muslim farmers, later called mudéjares and Moriscos, who stayed on the land. Zaragoza became its capital.
kingdom-of-aragon.e: The marriage of Petronila to Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona created the Crown of Aragon. Aragon kept its institutions under Habsburg Spain until Philip V abolished them by the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 after the War of the Spanish Succession.

kingdom-of-tamassos.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom built on rich copper mines, whose last king sold his realm to the king of Kition for fifty talents.
kingdom-of-tamassos.o: Tamassos lay in the Pediaios valley at the foot of the copper-rich Troodos mountains and was settled from the Bronze Age. Its copper may be the 'Temese' of Homer's Odyssey. By the 7th century BCE it was an independent kingdom; its king Admetus appears among the Cypriot rulers listed by Esarhaddon of Assyria.
kingdom-of-tamassos.r: The kingdom's wealth came from copper mining and smelting. Its royal tombs of the 6th century BCE are built of fine ashlar masonry imitating wooden houses, and a sanctuary of Apollo and the Mother of the Gods has yielded much sculpture. Tamassos used Greek and Phoenician alongside each other.
kingdom-of-tamassos.e: In the 4th century BCE King Pasicyprus sold Tamassos to Pumiyaton of the Kingdom of Kition for fifty talents. Alexander the Great later gave it to the king of Salamis. Tamassos survived as a town under Ptolemaic and Roman rule.

kingdom-of-surrey.t: A short-lived Saxon territory south of the Thames whose name, the 'southern district', survives as the county of Surrey.
kingdom-of-surrey.o: Surrey, Suthrige, probably began as the southern part of a larger Middle Saxon territory on both sides of the Thames. In the 7th century it lay between Kent, Wessex, Sussex and Mercia and was ruled by local leaders under one or another of them.
kingdom-of-surrey.r: The only known ruler is Frithuwold, a sub-king under Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia, who around 672 to 674 endowed Chertsey Abbey, founded by Bishop Eorcenwald. The charter shows estates, minsters and Mercian overlordship but no independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-surrey.e: Surrey never had a lasting royal line. Control passed between Mercia and Wessex, and in the 9th century it became a West Saxon shire, keeping its name and much of its boundary.

kingdom-of-york.t: The Viking kingdom centred on Jorvik, a prosperous Anglo-Scandinavian town whose kings were often also rulers of Dublin.
kingdom-of-york.o: The Great Heathen Army captured York in 866 to 867, and in 876 Halfdan shared out the land of Northumbria south of the Tees among his followers. Danish kings ruled from York, with Guthfrith in the 880s accepting Christianity. Early in the 10th century the Norse dynasty of the Kingdom of Dublin took over.
kingdom-of-york.r: Jorvik grew into a major town of craftsmen and traders, with goods from Scandinavia to the Middle East, as the Coppergate excavations show. Its kings minted coins, some with Christian symbols, and cooperated with the archbishops of York. Scandinavian settlement left hundreds of place-names across Yorkshire.
kingdom-of-york.e: Aethelstan seized York in 927, but Norse kings such as Olaf Guthfrithson, Amlaib Cuaran and Eric Bloodaxe returned repeatedly. Eric's expulsion and death in 954 ended the kingdom, and York became part of the Kingdom of England as an earldom.

kingdom-of-the-hwicce.t: An Anglo-Saxon sub-kingdom of the lower Severn valley around Worcester, ruled by its own kings under Mercian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.o: The Hwicce took shape in Gloucestershire, Worcestershire and western Warwickshire after the West Saxon victory at Dyrham in 577 opened the region to English settlement. By the 7th century the area was ruled by a local dynasty, possibly installed or confirmed by Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.r: Hwiccan kings such as Osric and Oshere founded minsters including Bath, Gloucester and Pershore, and a bishopric was created at Worcester around 680 to serve the people. The territory was rich in salt from Droitwich and in farmland, and its charters are among the earliest English documents.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.e: Hwiccan rulers were downgraded from kings to ealdormen in the late 8th century under Offa. The kingdom's boundaries survived as the medieval diocese of Worcester, preserving its outline for centuries.

kingdom-of-kourion.t: Cypriot kingdom on a clifftop above the south coast, remembered for the sanctuary of Apollo Hylates and for its king's betrayal at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE.
kingdom-of-kourion.o: Kourion arose in the Episkopi area of southern Cyprus, near a Late Bronze Age settlement, in the 11th century BCE. Its Greek inhabitants claimed descent from settlers from Argos. By the 7th century BCE it was one of the island's city-kingdoms, listed among the Cypriot rulers who paid tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon.
kingdom-of-kourion.r: The kings ruled a fertile territory along the Kouris river. The sanctuary of Apollo Hylates, god of the woodland, was its chief cult centre, and rich tombs yielded the gold and silver of the so-called Kourion treasure. Kourion followed the Cypriot syllabary and Greek institutions, under Assyrian and then Achaemenid overlordship.
kingdom-of-kourion.e: In the Ionian Revolt, King Stasanor deserted to the Persians at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE. Later King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre. The monarchy was abolished under Ptolemy I c. 312 BCE, and Kourion flourished as a Roman and early Christian city until earthquakes in the 4th century CE.
kingdom-of-kourion.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Hylates

kingdom-of-marion.t: Cypriot kingdom on the north-west coast that grew rich on copper trade with Athens until Ptolemy I destroyed it in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-marion.o: Marion grew near modern Polis Chrysochous in north-west Cyprus, close to the copper mines of Limni, in the early Iron Age. It emerged as a city-kingdom in the Cypro-Archaic period, facing Anatolia and the Aegean across the sea.
kingdom-of-marion.r: Marion exported copper and imported large quantities of Athenian painted pottery, found in its cemeteries. Its kings, some with Greek names such as Stasioikos and others possibly Phoenician, issued coins in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. Inscriptions use the Cypriot syllabary for Greek.
kingdom-of-marion.e: Its last king, Stasioikos II, sided with Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who destroyed Marion in 312 BCE and moved its people to Paphos. Ptolemy II refounded the site as Arsinoe c. 270 BCE, and the modern town of Polis stands there today.

kingdom-of-pengwern.t: A shadowy British kingdom of the Shropshire borderlands, remembered in the Welsh poems lamenting Cynddylan and the ruin of his hall.
kingdom-of-pengwern.o: Pengwern is known almost entirely from Welsh poetry, notably the Canu Heledd, a 9th or 10th century cycle of poems lamenting Cynddylan, a 7th century prince. Its centre is uncertain; later tradition placed it at Shrewsbury, while scholars suggest the Wrekin area or Din Gwrygon.
kingdom-of-pengwern.r: Nothing reliable is recorded of its government. The poems describe Cynddylan's hall at Eglwysau Bassa and his wars against the English, and he may have been an ally of Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia. The kingdom was probably one of several successors to the Cornovii tribal region.
kingdom-of-pengwern.e: Pengwern seems to have fallen to Mercian expansion in the mid 7th century; Cynddylan's death is lamented in the poems. Its lands became Mercian, while its memory survived in Welsh literature as a symbol of loss.

kingdom-of-tethba.t: A midland Irish kingdom spanning Longford and Westmeath, held by branches of the southern Ui Neill and later by the O'Farrells and O'Quinns.
kingdom-of-tethba.o: Tethba appears in the earliest Irish annals as a territory in the Irish midlands, divided by the River Inny into northern and southern parts. Its rulers in the early medieval period came from Cairpre and Maine, sons of Niall of the Nine Hostages, making it part of the southern Ui Neill world centred on Mide.
kingdom-of-tethba.r: Tethba was a small overkingship of several local peoples, often subordinate to the kings of Mide. Monasteries such as Ardagh and Clonmacnoise's daughter houses stood in or near its lands. In the 11th and 12th centuries local families, the Ui Cuinn and the Ui Fergail, rose to power in the northern part, later known as Annaly.
kingdom-of-tethba.e: After the Norman invasion much of southern Tethba was granted to Hugh de Lacy within the Lordship of Meath. Annaly survived under the O'Farrells until the 16th century, when it became County Longford.

knidos.t: Dorian port city on a Carian peninsula, home of Praxiteles's Aphrodite, the astronomer Eudoxus and a renowned school of medicine.
knidos.o: Dorian Greeks settled Knidos at the tip of a long peninsula in south-west Anatolia in the early first millennium BCE. It belonged to the Dorian Hexapolis with Kos, Halicarnassus and the three Rhodian cities of Lindos, Ialysos and Kamiros, which met at the sanctuary of Apollo at Triopion in Knidian territory.
knidos.r: Knidos was an oligarchy run by a council of sixty, and grew rich on trade, wine and its double harbour. When the Persian general Harpagus advanced c. 545 BCE, the Knidians tried to cut through their isthmus but submitted. The city later produced the astronomer Eudoxus, the physician Ctesias and Sostratus, architect of the Pharos of Alexandria; its treasury and clubhouse stood at Delphi.
knidos.e: Off Knidos in 394 BCE Conon's Persian-backed fleet destroyed Spartan sea power. In the 4th century BCE the city moved to the cape, where Praxiteles's nude Aphrodite drew visitors. It joined the Roman province of Asia in 129 BCE as a free city.

kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.t: The Gaelic lordship of north-west Ulster, ruled from the 13th century by the O'Donnells, whose flight in 1607 ended independent Gaelic rule in Ulster.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.o: Tir Chonaill, the land of Conall, was named after Conall Gulban, a son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. His descendants, the Cenel Conaill, formed one branch of the northern Ui Neill and held much of present-day County Donegal. Columba of Iona belonged to this kindred, which also shared the high kingship in the early centuries.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.r: Cenel Conaill kings alternated the northern overkingship with Cenel nEogain until the 8th century. From the 13th century the O'Donnell family ruled from Donegal Castle, with a strong fleet, Scottish mercenaries and learned bardic families such as the O'Clerys. Franciscan Donegal Friary was a key patron foundation.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.e: Red Hugh O'Donnell joined Hugh O'Neill in the Nine Years' War against England. After defeat, Rory O'Donnell, Earl of Tyrconnell, left Ireland in the Flight of the Earls in 1607, and his lands were confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster under the Kingdom of Ireland.

kingdom-of-waterford.t: A Norse town-kingdom at the mouth of the Suir, the oldest city in Ireland, until its storming by the Anglo-Normans in 1170.
kingdom-of-waterford.o: Vikings raided the south-east in the 9th century, and in 914 a large fleet under Ragnall established a base at Waterford, Vedrafjordr. The settlement grew into a fortified trading town ruled by Norse kings or jarls, sometimes linked to the Kingdom of Dublin.
kingdom-of-waterford.r: Waterford traded wine, slaves and goods across the Irish Sea and to France. Its rulers became Christian and accepted bishops consecrated at Canterbury from 1096. Irish overkings of Munster, especially the O'Briens, often controlled the town, and Reginald's Tower recalls its Norse defences.
kingdom-of-waterford.e: In 1170 Strongbow and Raymond le Gros stormed the town, and Strongbow married Aoife, daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, there. Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171 and made it a royal city in the Lordship of Ireland.

kingdom-of-iarmumu.t: The early medieval kingdom of West Munster around Killarney's lakes, ruled by the Eoganacht Locha Lein, rivals of the Munster kings at Cashel.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.o: Iarmumu took shape in south-west Ireland by the 6th century, when the Eoganacht Locha Lein, a branch of the dynasties ruling Munster, established themselves around Loch Lein, the Lower Lake at Killarney. Their territory covered much of later Kerry and west Cork, absorbing earlier peoples such as the Corcu Duibne.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.r: The kings of Iarmumu sometimes claimed the kingship of all Munster, but were usually excluded from the rotation of Cashel's Eoganacht branches. Inisfallen on Loch Lein became an important monastery, later home of the Annals of Inisfallen. Cattle wealth and client peoples supported the dynasty.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.e: By the 8th and 9th centuries the dynasty weakened, and other lineages gained ground in Kerry, notably the Ui Donnchada. In the 12th century the area fell within the Kingdom of Desmond under the MacCarthys, with the O'Donoghues as local lords around Killarney.

kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.t: A tiny Jutish kingdom on the Isle of Wight, the last part of England to accept Christianity, ended by the violent conquest of Caedwalla in 686.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.o: Bede reports that the Isle of Wight, like Kent and part of Hampshire, was settled by Jutes. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle claims that Cerdic and Cynric took the island in 530 and gave it to their kinsmen Stuf and Wihtgar, but the story is largely legendary.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.r: The Wihtwara lived from farming and the sea under their own kings, sometimes dependents of greater neighbours. In 661 Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia gave the island to the South Saxon king Aethelwealh. The island was still pagan in the 680s.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.e: In 686 Caedwalla of the Kingdom of Wessex conquered the island, killed King Arwald and had his two young brothers executed after baptism, as Bede recounts. The island became part of Wessex and was converted by Wilfrid's clergy.

kingdom-of-mercia.t: The great midland kingdom that dominated England in the 8th century under Aethelbald and Offa, whose Dyke still marks the Welsh border.
kingdom-of-mercia.o: Mercia, the 'border people', arose among Angles in the upper Trent valley. Later genealogies place its first kings, Icel and Creoda, in the 6th century, but the first well-attested ruler is the pagan Penda, who fought Northumbria and East Anglia from the 620s to his death at the Winwaed in 655.
kingdom-of-mercia.r: Mercian kings ruled from Tamworth, with a bishopric at Lichfield, and dominated client kingdoms such as the Hwicce and the Magonsaete. Offa took the title king of the English, issued a reformed silver penny, corresponded with Charlemagne and built Offa's Dyke. He briefly created an archbishopric at Lichfield.
kingdom-of-mercia.e: Defeat by Wessex at Ellendun in 825 and the Viking conquests of the 870s split Mercia. Its western half, under Aethelred and Aethelflaed, the Lady of the Mercians, allied with Wessex. After Aethelflaed's death in 918 it was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons.

kingdom-of-lindsey.t: A small Anglian kingdom in north Lincolnshire centred on Roman Lincoln, briefly fought over by Northumbria and Mercia before Mercian absorption.
kingdom-of-lindsey.o: Lindsey took its name from the Roman Lindum (Lincoln), and Anglian settlers established a kingdom there in the late 5th or 6th century. A list of its kings survives in a collection of royal genealogies, tracing them to Woden, ending with Aldfrith in the late 8th century.
kingdom-of-lindsey.r: The kingdom lay between the Humber and the Witham, bounded by fen and sea, and was too small to stand alone. Paulinus preached at Lincoln around 628 under Northumbrian protection, building a stone church. A separate bishopric of Lindsey was founded in 678.
kingdom-of-lindsey.e: Northumbria and Mercia contested Lindsey until the Battle of the Trent in 679 left it permanently Mercian. Its kings faded into dependent rulers and disappeared by about 800. The district was later settled by Danes and formed part of Lincolnshire.

kingdom-of-pergamon.t: Hellenistic kingdom of the Attalid dynasty in western Anatolia, a great centre of art and learning that was bequeathed to Rome in 133 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.o: Philetaerus, an officer guarding Lysimachus' treasure of 9,000 talents at the citadel of Pergamon, changed sides to Seleucus I in 282 BCE and kept the fortress and money. His nephew Eumenes I asserted independence from the Seleucids. Attalus I took the title of king around 238 BCE after defeating the Galatians.
kingdom-of-pergamon.r: The Attalids built Pergamon into a showpiece capital of terraces, temples and theatre, with a library second only to Alexandria's, traditionally linked to the development of parchment. The Great Altar of Zeus celebrated victory over the Galatians. Loyal alliance with Rome brought Eumenes II wide lands in Asia Minor after the Peace of Apamea in 188 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.e: Attalus III died in 133 BCE leaving his kingdom to Rome. Aristonicus, claiming to be a royal son, led a revolt that was crushed by 129 BCE, and the kingdom became the Roman province of Asia. The Pergamon Altar is now in Berlin.

kingdom-of-wessex.t: The kingdom of the West Saxons, which survived the Viking onslaught under Alfred the Great and grew into the Kingdom of England.
kingdom-of-wessex.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle traces Wessex to Cerdic and Cynric, said to have landed in 495 and taken the kingship in 519. Early kings of the Gewisse operated in the upper Thames valley before expanding west and south. Archaeology suggests more complex origins than the Chronicle's story.
kingdom-of-wessex.r: Wessex was divided into shires under ealdormen, with royal estates, law codes from Ine around 694, and bishoprics at Winchester and Sherborne. Christianity arrived with Birinus in 635. Victory over Mercia at Ellendun in 825 made Ecgberht the leading southern king. Alfred built a network of fortified burhs, a navy and a revival of learning in English.
kingdom-of-wessex.e: Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878 and his successors reconquered the Danelaw. From 886 Wessex merged into the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons, and under Aethelstan in 927 it became the core of the Kingdom of England, with Winchester its royal centre.

kingdom-of-bernicia.t: The northern Anglian kingdom based on the fortress of Bamburgh, whose kings united with Deira to create Northumbria.
kingdom-of-bernicia.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates Bernicia to 547, when Ida took the kingship and built Bamburgh. Its people were Angles who settled the coast between the Tees and the Forth among the British population. The British name Bryneich suggests the kingdom took over an earlier British territory.
kingdom-of-bernicia.r: Bernicia's kings were warriors whose power rested on tribute and plunder. Aethelfrith defeated Aedan of Dal Riata at Degsastan in 603 and the Britons at Chester, then seized Deira. His son Oswald brought Aidan from Iona, who founded Lindisfarne in 635, and royal sites such as Yeavering show grand halls.
kingdom-of-bernicia.e: Under Oswiu, Bernicia and the Kingdom of Deira were joined permanently after 654, forming the Kingdom of Northumbria. Bamburgh remained a royal fortress and later the seat of the Earldom of Bamburgh.

kingdom-of-athamania.t: Small mountain kingdom on the borders of Epirus and Thessaly whose king Amynander played the Roman, Macedonian and Seleucid powers off against each other.
kingdom-of-athamania.o: The Athamanians were a people of the Pindus mountains around the upper Achelous, between Epirus, Thessaly and Aetolia. Little is known of their early history. Under Macedonian and Epirote dominance they had their own kings, and the kingdom became visible in the later 3rd century BCE, with its royal seat at Argithea.
kingdom-of-athamania.r: Athamania was a pastoral highland realm of villages and fortified hilltop towns. Its importance came from its position on routes between Thessaly and western Greece. King Amynander joined Rome against Philip V of Macedon in 200-197 BCE and acted as an intermediary, then sided with Antiochus III in 191 BCE.
kingdom-of-athamania.e: Philip V overran Athamania in 191 BCE and Amynander fled to Ambracia. With Aetolian help he recovered his kingdom in 189 BCE, but it disappears from the record soon after and was absorbed into its neighbours. Knowledge of it comes almost entirely from Polybius and Livy.

kingdom-of-arles.t: The united kingdom of Burgundy and Provence, stretching from Basel to the Mediterranean, that became the third crown of the Holy Roman emperors.
kingdom-of-arles.o: Around 933 Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy acquired the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy from Hugh of Arles, uniting the lands between the Jura and the Mediterranean. His son Conrad the Peaceful ruled from 937 to 993 under the protection of Otto I, who had taken the young king to his court.
kingdom-of-arles.r: Royal power was weak: counts, archbishops of Lyon, Vienne and Arles, and later lords such as the dauphins of Viennois and counts of Provence held real authority. When the childless Rudolf III died in 1032, the kingdom passed to Emperor Conrad II. Frederick Barbarossa was crowned at Arles in 1178 and Charles IV in 1365.
kingdom-of-arles.e: French influence grew steadily along the Rhône. In 1378 Charles IV made the French Dauphin, the future Charles VI, imperial vicar of the kingdom for life, effectively ending imperial rule there. Its lands were gradually absorbed by the Kingdom of France and Savoy.

kingdom-of-the-isles.t: A Norse-Gaelic sea kingdom of Man and the Hebrides, ruled from the Isle of Man by the Crovan dynasty under Norwegian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-isles.o: Godred Crovan, a Norse-Gael who had fought at Stamford Bridge in 1066, seized the Isle of Man in 1079 after a battle at Sky Hill. His descendants ruled Man and the Hebrides, the Sudreys, as a kingdom under the nominal overlordship of Norway.
kingdom-of-the-isles.r: The kingdom was a maritime power of galleys and island fortresses, with Castle Rushen and the church at Rushen Abbey. Man's Tynwald assembly descends from its Norse institutions. Its kings intervened in Irish and Scottish affairs. Somerled's revolt in 1156 took the southern Hebrides, leaving the Crovan line with Man, Lewis and Skye.
kingdom-of-the-isles.e: After the Battle of Largs in 1263, Norway ceded Man and the Isles to the Kingdom of Scotland by the Treaty of Perth in 1266, the year after the last king, Magnus Olafsson, died. Man later came under English rule as the Lordship of Mann.

kingdom-of-salamis.t: The leading city-kingdom of ancient Cyprus, whose king Evagoras I united much of the island and defied the Persian Empire for a decade.
kingdom-of-salamis.o: Salamis was founded on the east coast of Cyprus in the 11th century BCE, succeeding nearby Enkomi as its harbour silted up. Greek tradition named Teucer, brother of Ajax, as its founder. Its royal tombs of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, with chariots and sacrificed horses, recall Homeric burial customs.
kingdom-of-salamis.r: The kings of Salamis were often the most powerful on Cyprus. Evelthon struck the island's first coins in the 6th century BCE, and Onesilus led the Cypriot revolt against Persia in 498 BCE. Evagoras I, who reigned from 411 to 374 BCE, promoted Greek culture, allied with Athens and fought the Achaemenid Empire until a negotiated peace in 380 BCE.
kingdom-of-salamis.e: The last king, Nicocreon, allied with Ptolemy I and died c. 310 BCE, and in 306 BCE Demetrius Poliorcetes won a great naval battle off Salamis. The kingdom then passed under the Ptolemaic Empire. Salamis remained a major city, renamed Constantia, until abandoned after the Arab raids of the 7th century CE.

kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.t: The kingdom of Provence founded by Boso in 879, the first realm in the Carolingian West to elect a king from outside the Carolingian family.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.o: In 879, after the deaths of Louis the Stammerer, bishops and nobles meeting at Mantaille elected Boso, a brother-in-law of Charles the Bald, as king of the lands around Vienne, Lyon and Provence. The Carolingian kings besieged Vienne in 880–882, but Boso's family kept control of the Rhône valley.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.r: The kingdom was a loose union of counties along the Rhône and in Provence, governed from Vienne with strong support from the bishops. Boso's son Louis the Blind was crowned emperor in Rome in 901 but was captured and blinded by Berengar of Italy in 905. Afterwards real power lay with his kinsman Hugh of Arles.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.e: Hugh of Arles, busy with his ambitions as king of Italy, gave up his claims to Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy around 933. The two Burgundian kingdoms were then united as the Kingdom of Arles, which later passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.t: The realm created by Alfred the Great and his son Edward, joining Wessex and English Mercia into the direct ancestor of the Kingdom of England.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.o: In 886 Alfred occupied London and, according to the Chronicle, all the English not under the Danes submitted to him. His charters began to use the title king of the Anglo-Saxons, uniting the Kingdom of Wessex with western Mercia under Aethelred, Lord of the Mercians, who married Alfred's daughter Aethelflaed.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.r: The kingdom was defended by burhs and a reorganised army. Alfred issued a law code and sponsored translations of Latin works into English. Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed reconquered the southern Danelaw, including the Five Boroughs and Danish East Anglia, between 910 and 920.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.e: After Aethelflaed's death Edward absorbed Mercia in 918. In 927 his son Aethelstan took York and received the submission of northern rulers, becoming the first king of the Kingdom of England.

kos.t: Dorian island state off Anatolia, birthplace of Hippocrates and home of the famous healing sanctuary of Asclepius.
kos.o: Kos, an island off the Carian coast near Halicarnassus, was settled from the Bronze Age, with Mycenaean remains. Dorian Greeks occupied it in the early Iron Age, and it joined the Dorian Hexapolis with Knidos, Halicarnassus and the Rhodian cities. Its first chief town was Astypalaia in the south-west.
kos.r: Kos was known for wine and fine translucent silk cloth. Hippocrates was born there c. 460 BCE and the Coan school of medicine bears his name. After Persian rule the island joined the Delian League. In 366 BCE the Coans founded a new capital on the north-east tip, and the Asclepieion was later built nearby.
kos.e: Kos was a favoured base of the Ptolemaic Empire, where Ptolemy II was born and the poet Philitas taught. It later allied with Rome and became part of the province of Asia in 129 BCE, remaining a free city prized for its sanctuary.

kingdom-of-paphos.t: Ancient Cypriot kingdom centred on the great sanctuary of Aphrodite, whose kings served as the goddess's high priests for some eight centuries.
kingdom-of-paphos.o: Paphos grew at Palaepaphos, modern Kouklia, a Late Bronze Age town in south-west Cyprus. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE Aegean settlers arrived, and Greek legend credited Agapenor of Tegea with founding the city after the Trojan War. An inscription of the 11th century BCE shows Greek already written there.
kingdom-of-paphos.r: Its kings combined royal power with the priesthood of the Paphian goddess, later identified with Aphrodite, whose open-air sanctuary with a conical stone drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean. Paphos used the Cypriot syllabary for Greek and struck its own coins. It paid tribute to Assyria and later to the Achaemenid Empire, and joined the revolt against Persia in 498 BCE.
kingdom-of-paphos.e: The last king, Nicocles, founded the harbour city of Nea Paphos, which became the capital of Ptolemaic and Roman Cyprus. The kingdom was abolished when Ptolemy I took the island, by c. 306 BCE, but the sanctuary of Aphrodite flourished into late antiquity.

kingdom-of-east-anglia.t: The kingdom of the East Angles in Norfolk and Suffolk, famed for the Sutton Hoo ship burial and for its martyred last king, Edmund.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.o: Angles settled Norfolk and Suffolk in the 5th century, and the Wuffingas dynasty, named after Wuffa, ruled by the 6th century. Its royal centre lay at Rendlesham in the Deben valley, close to the burial ground at Sutton Hoo.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.r: Raedwald, overlord of the southern English around 616, probably lies in the Sutton Hoo ship burial, with its gold and Byzantine silver. He kept both a Christian altar and a pagan one. Later kings founded the bishopric at Dunwich under Felix and monasteries such as Ely. Ipswich became one of the first post-Roman towns.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.e: East Anglia was often under Mercian overlordship in the 8th century. The Great Heathen Army killed King Edmund in 869 and the Danes later settled the land as the Danish Kingdom of East Anglia. Edmund's cult grew at Bury St Edmunds.

kingdom-of-alashiya.t: Late Bronze Age kingdom on Cyprus whose rulers traded copper with Egypt, the Hittites and Ugarit, as revealed by the Amarna letters.
kingdom-of-alashiya.o: Alashiya appears in Near Eastern texts from the 18th century BCE as a source of copper, and most scholars identify it with Cyprus or part of it. Cyprus developed urban centres in the Late Cypriot period from c. 1650 BCE, including Enkomi on the east coast, Kalavasos and Alassa, though which was the royal seat is uncertain.
kingdom-of-alashiya.r: The king of Alashiya corresponded with Pharaoh Akhenaten as a 'brother' in the Amarna letters, sending copper ingots in return for silver, oil and luxury goods. Clay analysis shows these letters were made on Cyprus. Enkomi had copper workshops and ashlar buildings, and the island used the Cypro-Minoan script. The Hittite Empire claimed overlordship in the 13th century BCE.
kingdom-of-alashiya.e: Letters from Ugarit describe enemy ships threatening Alashiya c. 1200 BCE, and Suppiluliuma II fought naval battles off its coast. In the following century Cypriot towns declined or moved, Aegean settlers arrived, and the island reorganised into the Iron Age kingdoms such as Salamis, Paphos and Kition.

kingdom-of-desmond.t: The MacCarthy kingdom of South Munster, created when Munster was split in 1118 and surviving in parts until the end of the 16th century.
kingdom-of-desmond.o: The Treaty of Glanmire in 1118 divided Munster, giving the south, Deasmumu, to the MacCarthys, heirs of the Eoganacht kings of Cashel. Cormac MacCarthy ruled from Cork and built Cormac's Chapel on the Rock of Cashel, consecrated in 1134.
kingdom-of-desmond.r: Desmond's kings lost much of Cork to the Normans after 1177, but Finghin MacCarthy's victory at Callann in 1261 halted the colonists. The MacCarthy Mor branch then ruled from Pallis in Kerry, with cadet lines in Carbery and Muskerry. The kingdom was an overlordship of Gaelic lords such as the O'Sullivans and O'Donoghues.
kingdom-of-desmond.e: Donal MacCarthy Mor became Earl of Clancare in 1565 under the Kingdom of Ireland. His death without a legitimate male heir in 1596 ended the senior line, and its lands passed into English plantations.

kingdom-of-the-regni.t: Client kingdom of Togidubnus in Sussex and Hampshire, a loyal ally of Rome after the conquest whose seat may have been the palace at Fishbourne.
kingdom-of-the-regni.o: After the Roman invasion of 43, much of the former realm of the Atrebates (Britain) was entrusted to Togidubnus, a British noble loyal to Rome. Tacitus says that certain states were given to him and that he remained faithful down to his own day, and the region became a base for Roman operations along the south coast.
kingdom-of-the-regni.r: An inscription from Chichester dedicating a temple to Neptune and Minerva names Tiberius Claudius Togidubnus as great king in Britain, showing that he held Roman citizenship and royal status. His capital, Noviomagus Reginorum, grew into a Roman-style town, and the lavish villa at Fishbourne, with mosaics and formal gardens, has often been linked to him. The kingdom provided Rome with a stable and Romanised territory.
kingdom-of-the-regni.e: When Togidubnus died, probably around 80, the client kingdom was absorbed into the province of Roman Britain. Its lands were divided into civitates, the Regni around Chichester and probably the Belgae (Britain) around Winchester. Chichester remains the main town of the region.

kingdom-of-moylurg.t: A Gaelic lordship of north Roscommon ruled by the MacDermots from their island fortress on Lough Key.
kingdom-of-moylurg.o: Magh Luirg was the territory of a branch of the Sil Muiredaig, the ruling kindred of Connacht. In the 12th century the MacDermot family, descended from Diarmait mac Taidg, emerged as its rulers and as marshals of the O'Connor kings of Connacht.
kingdom-of-moylurg.r: The MacDermots ruled from the Rock of Lough Ce, an island fortress on Lough Key, and patronised the abbey of Boyle and the learned families who compiled the Annals of Loch Ce. Their lordship was based on cattle, clients and armed retainers, and they served as kingmakers in Connacht politics.
kingdom-of-moylurg.e: The Composition of Connacht in 1585 brought the lordship under English land law. The MacDermots kept part of their lands and their title, the MacDermot, Prince of Coolavin, has been recognised into modern times.

kingdom-of-lapethos.t: North Cypriot kingdom where Phoenician kings ruled a Greek population in the Classical age, until Ptolemy I deposed the last king in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-lapethos.o: Lapethos lay on the north coast of Cyprus near modern Lambousa, facing Anatolia. Greek tradition said it was founded by Praxandros from Laconia after the Trojan War. A city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE, it had close ties with the Phoenician coast.
kingdom-of-lapethos.r: In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE Lapethos was ruled by a dynasty with Phoenician names, such as Sidqmelek, who issued coins with Phoenician legends; Phoenician inscriptions from the town honour Melqart and other gods. The economy rested on farming, fishing and trade, and the city had a good harbour.
kingdom-of-lapethos.e: Its last king, Praxippos, supported Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who removed him in 312 BCE and annexed the kingdom. Lapethos continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman town, later called Lambousa, abandoned after Arab raids in the 7th century CE.

kingdom-of-pylos.t: Mycenaean kingdom of Messenia whose burnt palace preserved more than a thousand Linear B tablets, the fullest record of a Bronze Age Greek state.
kingdom-of-pylos.o: Pylos grew on the Englianos ridge in western Messenia, where rich shaft and tholos tombs show an emerging elite by c. 1650 BCE, including the Griffin Warrior burial found in 2015. By the 14th and 13th centuries BCE its rulers had unified Messenia into a single kingdom divided into two provinces.
kingdom-of-pylos.r: The palace, linked by Homer with King Nestor, was headed by a wanax with a lawagetas below him. Its Linear B archive records taxation of some 16 districts, landholding, bronze-smiths, flax and perfumed oil production, rowers for the fleet and offerings to Poseidon, Zeus, Hera and the Potnia. Frescoes and a well-preserved throne room survive.
kingdom-of-pylos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire c. 1180 BCE, apparently while preparing coastal defences, and the region largely depopulated. Its tablets, baked by the fire, were found by Carl Blegen in 1939 and helped Michael Ventris show in 1952 that Linear B was Greek.

kingdom-of-circinn.t: A Pictish kingdom or province in the area of Angus and the Mearns, named in early Irish annals and in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
kingdom-of-circinn.o: Circinn appears as one of the seven Pictish provinces in the origin legend that named them after the sons of Cruithne, and in Irish annals, which record a battle of Circinn in 598. It is usually placed in Angus and the Mearns, south of the Mounth.
kingdom-of-circinn.r: Almost nothing is known of its government. It was probably one of the regional lordships within the Pictish kingdom, and the fertile lowlands of Angus held important royal and church sites such as Forteviot's neighbours, Aberlemno and later Brechin, with their carved Pictish stones.
kingdom-of-circinn.e: Circinn's identity merged into the Kingdom of Scotland when Pictland became Alba in the 9th and 10th centuries. The later earldoms of Angus and the Mearns may continue its territory.

kingdom-of-mycenae.t: The leading Bronze Age Greek kingdom in the Argolid, whose shaft graves, Lion Gate and tholos tombs gave its name to the Mycenaean civilisation.
kingdom-of-mycenae.o: Mycenae occupies a hill in the north-east Argolid controlling routes to Corinth. Its rise is shown by Grave Circles A and B, used c. 1650 to 1500 BCE, with gold masks and weapons. In the 14th and 13th centuries BCE a palace, Cyclopean walls and great tholos tombs such as the Treasury of Atreus were built.
kingdom-of-mycenae.r: Mycenae was ruled by a wanax from a palace with a central megaron and frescoes, and was probably the most powerful of several Argolid centres including Tiryns. Linear B tablets record perfumed oil and other goods. Its pottery spread across the Mediterranean, and some scholars link it to the Ahhiyawa known from Hittite texts. The Lion Gate dates to c. 1250 BCE.
kingdom-of-mycenae.e: The citadel suffered destructions c. 1200 BCE and the palace system collapsed, though occupation continued until c. 1100 BCE. Later the small town was destroyed by Argos c. 468 BCE. Homer made it the seat of Agamemnon, and Schliemann's excavations from 1876 made it famous.

kingdom-of-idalion.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom famous for the Idalion Tablet, a bronze contract recording how the city paid a doctor to treat the wounded during a siege.
kingdom-of-idalion.o: Idalion grew on the hills of central Cyprus, near the copper-bearing foothills of Troodos, in the early Iron Age. By the 7th century BCE it was a city-kingdom listed among Cypriot states paying tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon. Its acropolis held sanctuaries of the goddesses later called Athena and Aphrodite.
kingdom-of-idalion.r: Idalion controlled copper production and fertile land. The Idalion Tablet, a bronze plaque of the early 5th century BCE written in the Cypriot syllabary, records that King Stasicypros and the city granted land to the physician Onasilos and his brothers for treating those wounded when 'the Medes and the Kitians' besieged the town.
kingdom-of-idalion.e: Idalion was conquered by the Phoenician Kingdom of Kition c. 450 BCE and lost its independence, Kition then ruling it with Phoenician administration. The town continued under Ptolemaic and Roman rule but declined.

kingdom-of-viguera.t: A short-lived sub-kingdom in La Rioja, carved out of Pamplona for a royal younger son and soon folded back into the realm of Navarre.
kingdom-of-viguera.o: Around 970 King Sancho II Garcés of Pamplona, following the will of his father García Sánchez I, granted the Rioja lands around Viguera to his younger brother Ramiro Garcés with the title of king. The territory, recently won from the Muslims, guarded the upper Ebro and the approaches to Nájera.
kingdom-of-viguera.r: Viguera was an appanage rather than a fully independent state: its kings acknowledged the senior line in Pamplona and fought alongside it against the Caliphate of Córdoba. Ramiro is said to have died at the Battle of Torrevicente in 981. Charters show his sons Sancho Ramírez and García Ramírez styled as kings, though little else is recorded.
kingdom-of-viguera.e: After the line of Ramiro faded out in the early 11th century, Viguera was reabsorbed into the Kingdom of Navarre, by then under Sancho III the Great. It survives chiefly as a case study in how Iberian kings provided for younger sons with subordinate royal titles.

kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.t: The O'Neill kingdom of mid-Ulster, the most powerful Gaelic lordship of late medieval Ireland, whose last ruler led the Nine Years' War.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.o: Tir Eoghain, 'Eogan's land', descends from the Cenel nEogain, the northern Ui Neill kindred traced to Eogan, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. After the decline of the Mac Lochlainn line in the late 12th century, the O'Neills emerged as kings, ruling from Dungannon with inaugurations at Tullyhogue.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.r: The O'Neills dominated Ulster, taking tribute from lesser lords such as the O'Cahans and Maguires. Their power rested on cattle, a large army including Scottish gallowglasses, and a court of poets and lawyers. Conn Bacach O'Neill became Earl of Tyrone in 1542, but conflict with the crown continued under Shane O'Neill.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.e: Hugh O'Neill led the Nine Years' War against England, but defeat at Kinsale in 1601 forced his submission. He left in the Flight of the Earls in 1607, and Tyrone was confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster in the Kingdom of Ireland.

kingdom-of-scotland.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom of the Scots, forged from Pictland and Dal Riata, which kept its independence until the Union with England in 1707.
kingdom-of-scotland.o: Tradition dates the kingdom to Kenneth MacAlpin, who ruled the Picts from about 843. The Pictish and Gaelic realms merged into the kingdom of Alba by around 900, centred on Scone and Dunkeld. It expanded over Lothian, Strathclyde, and in 1266 the Western Isles from Norway.
kingdom-of-scotland.r: Scotland developed royal burghs, feudal lordship and a church of its own under David I. The Wars of Independence, with William Wallace and Robert the Bruce's victory at Bannockburn in 1314, secured independence. The Stewart monarchy followed in 1371, Edinburgh became the capital, and the Reformation of 1560 created a Presbyterian church.
kingdom-of-scotland.e: In 1603 James VI inherited England, joining the crowns. The Acts of Union of 1707 merged the Scottish and English parliaments into the Kingdom of Great Britain, though Scotland kept its own law, church and education.

kingdom-of-ergyng.t: A small British kingdom in the Wye valley around the Roman town of Ariconium, whose name survives in Archenfield, a Welsh-speaking district of Herefordshire.
kingdom-of-ergyng.o: Ergyng emerged after Roman rule ended, its name derived from Ariconium, an iron-working town near Ross-on-Wye. It appears in the 6th and 7th centuries in the charters of the Book of Llandaff, which name local kings such as Peibio, associated in legend with the birth of Saint Dubricius.
kingdom-of-ergyng.r: Ergyng was a Christian British kingdom in which churches and monasteries, many linked to Dubricius, held land through royal grants. Its rulers were at times linked to the dynasties of Gwent and Glywysing. Little else is reliably known of its government.
kingdom-of-ergyng.e: From the 7th century the kingdom was absorbed by Gwent, and English settlement from Mercia advanced into the area. By the 10th century it was the district of Archenfield, under English lordship but still Welsh in law and speech; Domesday Book recorded its Welsh customs.

kingdom-of-france.t: The monarchy that grew from the Capetians' small domain around Paris into Europe's most populous and centralised state, ending with the Revolution.
kingdom-of-france.o: In 987 the magnates elected Hugh Capet, duke of the Franks, as king after the last Carolingian died. The early Capetians directly controlled only the Île-de-France and Orléans, while dukes and counts of Normandy, Aquitaine, Burgundy and Flanders were in practice independent.
kingdom-of-france.r: Kings slowly extended the royal domain by war, marriage and law: Philip II took Normandy in 1204, Louis IX became a model of Christian kingship, and the Valois survived the Hundred Years' War. After the Wars of Religion, Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. Louis XIV built absolute rule at Versailles, and French language and culture dominated Europe.
kingdom-of-france.e: Debt and political crisis led Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789, beginning the Revolution. The monarchy became constitutional in 1791 and was abolished in September 1792, replaced by the French First Republic; Louis XVI was executed in 1793.

kingdom-of-dublin.t: The Norse kingdom founded around Dublin's harbour, a hub of the Viking trade network that linked Ireland to Scandinavia, Britain and the slave markets.
kingdom-of-dublin.o: Vikings built a fortified base, the longphort, at Dublin in 841. From 853 the annals record Amlaib and later Imar, ancestors of a dynasty of kings who ruled both Dublin and, at times, the Kingdom of York. Expelled by the Irish in 902, they returned in 917.
kingdom-of-dublin.r: Dublin was a trading town of streets, houses and workshops, revealed by excavations at Wood Quay, dealing in slaves, silver, furs and craft goods. It minted coins from about 997. Its rulers converted to Christianity in the 10th century and Sitric Silkbeard founded Christ Church Cathedral around 1030. Irish kings often controlled it as a valuable prize.
kingdom-of-dublin.e: After defeat at Clontarf in 1014, Dublin was dominated by Irish overkings. In 1170 Strongbow and Diarmait Mac Murchada captured it, and in 1171 Henry II made it the capital of the Lordship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-dublin.re: Norse paganism; Christianity from the 10th century

kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.t: The Alpine kingdom of the Welf dynasty, founded at Saint-Maurice in 888, which later absorbed Provence to form the Kingdom of Arles.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.o: After the deposition of Emperor Charles the Fat in 888, the Welf noble Rudolf, margrave of Transjurane Burgundy, had himself crowned king at the abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune. His kingdom covered western Switzerland, the Jura and parts of Franche-Comté, and he held it against the East Frankish king Arnulf.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.r: The kings controlled the Great St Bernard pass and relied on rich abbeys such as Saint-Maurice and on alliances with local bishops at Lausanne, Geneva and Sion. Rudolf II was defeated by Swabia at Winterthur in 919, then reached for the Italian crown in the 920s before trading those claims for Provence.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.e: Around 933 Rudolf II obtained Lower Burgundy from Hugh of Arles, merging the two realms into the Kingdom of Arles. His son Conrad the Peaceful ruled the united kingdom under strong Ottonian influence, and in 1032 it passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-the-picts.t: Early medieval kingdom of northern and eastern Scotland, known for its carved symbol stones, which merged with the Gaels to form the kingdom of Alba.
kingdom-of-the-picts.o: The Picts are first named in a Roman panegyric of 297 as enemies of Britain alongside the Irish. The name, Latin for 'painted people', was applied to the peoples north of the Forth, descendants of the Caledonii, Maeatae and other Iron Age groups. Over the following centuries their many districts were drawn together under powerful over-kings.
kingdom-of-the-picts.r: The Picts left few written records but carved distinctive symbol stones with combs, mirrors, crescents and animals, later combined with Christian crosses. Kings such as Bridei son of Maelchon, visited by Columba in the 560s, ruled through regional lords. Bridei son of Beli defeated the Northumbrians at Dun Nechtain in 685, and Óengus son of Fergus dominated northern Britain in the 8th century. Christianity spread from Iona and Northumbria.
kingdom-of-the-picts.e: Viking attacks in the 9th century devastated the Pictish elite, notably in a great defeat in 839. Cináed mac Ailpín, a king of Gaelic descent, took power around 843, and by about 900 Pictland had become the Gaelic-speaking kingdom of Alba, the core of medieval Scotland.
kingdom-of-the-picts.re: Celtic polytheism; Christianity from the 6th century

kingdom-of-essex.t: The kingdom of the East Saxons north of the Thames, which controlled London for long periods and had a dynasty with unusual 'S' names.
kingdom-of-essex.o: The East Saxons settled Essex, Middlesex and parts of Hertfordshire. Their royal genealogy traces kings to Aescwine, traditionally placed in 527, and later kings bore names beginning with S, such as Saeberht, Sigeberht and Swithred.
kingdom-of-essex.r: Essex held London, which Bede called a market of many peoples. Saeberht accepted Christianity around 604 and Mellitus became bishop of London, but the kingdom reverted to paganism after his death until Cedd's mission in the 650s. Several kings often ruled jointly. Essex usually stood under the overlordship of Kent or Mercia.
kingdom-of-essex.e: After 825 Essex submitted to Ecgberht of the Kingdom of Wessex, and later fell within the Danelaw. In the 10th century it was absorbed into the Kingdom of England as a shire, which survives as the county of Essex.

kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.t: The short-lived sea realm of Somerled, who seized the southern Hebrides from the kings of Man and founded the dynasty of the Lords of the Isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.o: Somerled, a Norse-Gaelic warlord of Argyll married to a daughter of Olaf I of Man, challenged his brother-in-law Godred of the Kingdom of the Isles. After a sea battle in 1156 the Hebrides were divided, and in 1158 Somerled drove Godred from Man, ruling Argyll, Kintyre and the southern isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.r: Somerled's power rested on galley fleets and the loyalty of Gaelic and Norse-Gaelic kindreds. He acted as an independent ruler, sometimes allied with and sometimes against the Scottish king, and is linked with the founding of Saddell Abbey in Kintyre.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.e: Somerled was killed in 1164 at Renfrew while invading the Kingdom of Scotland. His realm was divided among his sons, ancestors of the MacDougalls, MacDonalds and MacRuairis, whose descendants later formed the Lordship of the Isles.

kingdom-of-england.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom unified by Aethelstan, transformed by the Norman Conquest and joined with Scotland in 1707.
kingdom-of-england.o: In 927 Aethelstan took York and received the submission of the northern rulers, completing the work of the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons. Viking kings briefly regained York until 954, and Danish kings Cnut and his sons ruled England from 1016 to 1042.
kingdom-of-england.r: Late Anglo-Saxon England had shires, a strong coinage and royal writs. After William the Conqueror's victory at Hastings in 1066, Norman lords, Domesday Book and a French-speaking elite reshaped society. Magna Carta in 1215, the growth of Parliament and common law, the wool trade and the Reformation under Henry VIII defined later centuries.
kingdom-of-england.e: England annexed Wales between 1283 and 1543 and ruled the Lordship of Ireland. James VI of Scotland inherited the crown in 1603, and after the Civil War and the Commonwealth of England, the Acts of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain.

kingdom-of-cornwall.t: The last surviving British kingdom of the south-west peninsula, which held out against Wessex until the 9th and 10th centuries.
kingdom-of-cornwall.o: Cornwall emerged as a separate British kingdom as the larger kingdom of Dumnonia shrank under West Saxon pressure. By the early 8th century Wessex had taken Devon, and the British realm beyond the Tamar became known as Kernow or Cornwall. Its kings are poorly recorded; Geraint fought Ine of Wessex around 710.
kingdom-of-cornwall.r: Cornwall kept its Brittonic language, saints' cults and links with Wales and Brittany. Tin mining and sea trade continued from Roman times. A defeat of a combined Cornish and Viking army at Hingston Down in 838 shows its kings still resisting the Kingdom of Wessex. The Annales Cambriae record the drowning of King Dungarth in 875.
kingdom-of-cornwall.e: Cornwall was brought under English control by the 9th century, and Aethelstan fixed the Tamar as the boundary around 936. It became part of the Kingdom of England, while the Cornish language survived into the 18th century.

kingdom-of-portugal.t: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, which fixed its borders by 1249, led the age of oceanic exploration and lasted until the revolution of 1910.
kingdom-of-portugal.o: The County of Portugal, a fief of León, passed to Afonso Henriques, who styled himself king after his victory at Ourique in 1139. León recognised him at Zamora in 1143 and the papacy in 1179. With crusader help he took Lisbon in 1147, and Afonso III completed the conquest of the Algarve in 1249.
kingdom-of-portugal.r: Portugal was a Catholic monarchy with Cortes, military orders and a strong maritime economy. After the victory of Aljubarrota in 1385, John I founded the Aviz dynasty, whose princes launched the voyages that created the Portuguese Empire. Pepper, Brazilian sugar and gold financed the crown. Manuel I ruled at the peak of the spice trade.
kingdom-of-portugal.e: The kingdom fell under Spanish kings in the Iberian Union from 1580 to 1640, then revived under the Braganzas. After the 1908 assassination of Carlos I, a revolution on 5 October 1910 ended the monarchy and created the First Portuguese Republic.

kingdom-of-soloi.t: Cypriot kingdom on Morphou Bay, said to have taken its name from the Athenian lawgiver Solon, who advised its king.
kingdom-of-soloi.o: Soloi lay on the bay of Morphou in north-western Cyprus, near the copper mines of Skouriotissa. Founded in the early Iron Age, it was a city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE. Plutarch tells that King Philocyprus moved the city to a better site on Solon's advice and named it after him.
kingdom-of-soloi.r: Soloi grew rich on copper and farmland. Its king Aristocyprus fell fighting the Persians at Salamis in 497 BCE, after which Soloi endured a five-month siege. The palace of Vouni on a nearby hill, built in the 5th century BCE, may have been used to watch over Soloi. King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre in 332 BCE.
kingdom-of-soloi.e: Its last king, Eunostos, married Eirene, daughter of Ptolemy I, and the kingdom was absorbed into Ptolemaic Cyprus c. 312 BCE. Soloi remained a city into Roman and early Christian times.

kingdom-of-brega.t: A kingdom of the southern Ui Neill on the fertile plain north of Dublin, home to Tara, Knowth and Newgrange and rival of Mide.
kingdom-of-brega.o: Brega emerged in the 7th century when the Sil nAedo Slaine, descendants of Aed Slaine of the southern Ui Neill, established themselves in the plain between the Liffey and the Boyne. Their rulers made the ancient passage tomb at Knowth into a royal residence.
kingdom-of-brega.r: Brega's kings shared the kingship of Tara with Clann Cholmain of Mide until the 8th century, but later lost out. The kingdom split into northern and southern parts. It contained monasteries such as Slane, Duleek and Monasterboice, and from the 9th century suffered heavy pressure from the Norse of the Kingdom of Dublin.
kingdom-of-brega.e: By the 11th century Brega was fragmented and dominated by Mide, Dublin and Leinster. Its lands passed into the Lordship of Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy in 1172, and its name survives in Irish place-names.

kingdom-of-northumbria.t: The kingdom of the Angles north of the Humber, home of Bede, Lindisfarne and the Northumbrian Renaissance, later carved up by the Vikings.
kingdom-of-northumbria.o: Northumbria grew out of the union of the Kingdom of Bernicia and the Kingdom of Deira, which became lasting under Oswiu after his victory over Penda at the Winwaed in 655. At its height it stretched from the Humber to the Firth of Forth and west to the Irish Sea.
kingdom-of-northumbria.r: Northumbrian kings were Christian patrons of monasteries such as Lindisfarne, Wearmouth-Jarrow and Whitby, where the Synod of 664 chose Roman over Irish church practice. This produced the Lindisfarne Gospels, the Codex Amiatinus and the works of Bede and Alcuin. The 8th century was marked by frequent royal murders and depositions.
kingdom-of-northumbria.e: Defeat by the Picts at Nechtansmere in 685 checked its northward growth, and Vikings sacked Lindisfarne in 793. In 867 the Great Heathen Army took York, creating the Kingdom of York, while English rulers held out at Bamburgh. The last Viking king, Eric Bloodaxe, was expelled in 954.

kingdom-of-thomond.t: The O'Brien kingdom of North Munster, descendant of Brian Boru's power base, which kept its independence until 1543.
kingdom-of-thomond.o: Thomond arose from the Dal Cais lands in Clare and Limerick. In 1118 the Treaty of Glanmire, imposed by Turlough O'Connor, split Munster, leaving the O'Briens with the north, Tuadmumu. Their capital was Limerick, the former Kingdom of Limerick.
kingdom-of-thomond.r: The O'Brien kings were patrons of churches such as Holy Cross, Killaloe and Limerick's cathedral, founded by Domnall Mor O'Brien. After losing Limerick to the Normans in the 1190s, they ruled from Clonroad near Ennis. In 1318 Muirchertach O'Brien defeated the Normans at Dysert O'Dea, preserving Gaelic rule west of the Shannon.
kingdom-of-thomond.e: In 1543 Murrough O'Brien surrendered his kingship to Henry VIII and became Earl of Thomond under the Kingdom of Ireland. His lands became County Clare in the 1570s.

kaulonia.t: Achaean Greek city on the Calabrian coast, a dependency of Croton, destroyed by Dionysius I of Syracuse in 389 BCE.
kaulonia.o: Kaulonia was founded in the 7th century BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, near modern Monasterace Marina, by Achaean settlers, probably sent out by Croton, to secure its southern border against Locri.
kaulonia.r: Kaulonia remained closely tied to Croton. Its silver coins, showing Apollo carrying a small running figure and a deer, are among the finest of Magna Graecia. Excavations have uncovered a Doric temple, walls and houses, and a large floor mosaic with a dragon of the 3rd century BCE. Little is known of its government.
kaulonia.e: After defeating the Italiote League at the Elleporus river in 389 BCE, Dionysius I took Kaulonia, moved its people to Syracuse and gave its land to Locri. A smaller town revived later but was destroyed during the wars with Pyrrhus and Hannibal, and by the Roman period the site was deserted.

kingdom-of-rheged.t: A British kingdom of the 'Old North' around the Solway, celebrated in Welsh poetry for King Urien and his battles against the Angles.
kingdom-of-rheged.o: Rheged emerged in the 6th century among the Brittonic kingdoms of northern Britain. Its location is uncertain, but scholars usually place it around Carlisle, Cumbria and Galloway. Its fame rests on poems attributed to Taliesin praising Urien Rheged, and on the Historia Brittonum.
kingdom-of-rheged.r: Urien is remembered as a leader of a coalition of British kings that besieged the Angles of Bernicia on Lindisfarne in the late 6th century, before he was murdered by a rival. Welsh tradition remembers the court as a centre of bardic patronage. Its society and economy are otherwise almost unknown.
kingdom-of-rheged.e: Rheged seems to have passed peacefully to Northumbria, perhaps through the marriage of Oswiu to Rhiainfellt, a descendant of Urien, around 638. Its memory lived on in Welsh poetry and Arthurian romance, where Urien and his son Owain became famous figures.

kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.t: A brief sub-kingdom in the east Midlands created for Penda's son Peada, notable as the place where Christianity first entered Mercian lands.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.o: The Middle Angles were a group of peoples in the east Midlands, around the Fens and the Nene and Welland valleys. Around 653 Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia made his son Peada their king. Peada married Alhflaed, a daughter of Oswiu of Northumbria, and accepted baptism as a condition of the marriage.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.r: Peada brought four priests, including Cedd and Diuma, who preached among the Middle Angles, the first Christian mission in Mercian territory. Tradition links Peada to the foundation of Medeshamstede, later Peterborough Abbey. The many small peoples of the region, listed in the Tribal Hidage, kept their own identities.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.e: After Penda's death in 655 Oswiu let Peada rule southern Mercia, but he was murdered in 656, allegedly through his wife's treachery. The Middle Angles were absorbed into Mercia, though they kept a bishopric at Leicester.

kingdom-of-mide.t: The midland kingdom around the sacred hill of Uisnech, ruled by the Clann Cholmain kings who often held the kingship of Tara.
kingdom-of-mide.o: Mide formed in the 6th century as the southern Ui Neill dynasties established themselves in the Irish midlands. The Clann Cholmain branch, descended from Colman Mor, emerged as its dominant line by the 8th century, ruling in what is now Westmeath with Uisnech as its symbolic centre.
kingdom-of-mide.r: Clann Cholmain kings alternated the kingship of Tara with the northern Ui Neill. Mael Sechnaill mac Maele Ruanaid and Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill were among the most powerful kings in Ireland. The kingdom contained great monasteries such as Durrow and Clonard, and royal sites at Lough Ennell.
kingdom-of-mide.e: After Brian Boru's rise, Mide was repeatedly partitioned by rival provincial kings. In 1172 Henry II granted it to Hugh de Lacy, creating the Lordship of Meath, and the native line survived only as minor lords.

kingdom-of-breifne.t: A Gaelic kingdom of the drumlin country of Leitrim and Cavan, ruled by the O'Rourkes, whose king Tigernan was a key player in the Norman invasion.
kingdom-of-breifne.o: Breifne emerged in the 8th century among the Ui Briuin of Connacht, whose branch, the Ui Briuin Breifne, settled the lakes and hills of later Leitrim and Cavan. The O'Rourke family became its leading dynasty by the 10th century.
kingdom-of-breifne.r: Breifne was an upland kingdom of cattle, lakes and crannog dwellings. Its kings occasionally claimed the kingship of Connacht. Tigernan Ua Ruairc, ruler from about 1124 to 1172, fought Diarmait Mac Murchada of Leinster, who had abducted his wife Derbforgaill; their feud helped bring the Normans to Ireland. Tigernan was killed at Tlachtga in 1172.
kingdom-of-breifne.e: After the death of its king in 1256, Breifne split between the O'Rourkes of West Breifne and the O'Reillys of East Breifne. Both survived until the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

kingdom-of-tiryns.t: Mycenaean citadel near the Argolic Gulf whose Cyclopean walls, among the most massive of the Bronze Age, so impressed later Greeks that they credited them to giants.
kingdom-of-tiryns.o: Tiryns stands on a low rock near the coast of the Argolid, settled from the Early Bronze Age, when a large circular building was erected on its summit. Mycenaean rulers built a fortified palace from c. 1600 BCE, and in the 14th and 13th centuries BCE the citadel was enclosed by walls up to 8 metres thick, with vaulted galleries.
kingdom-of-tiryns.r: The palace had a megaron with painted floors and frescoes of women in procession and boar hunts. Tiryns probably served as the harbour and partner, or subordinate, of nearby Mycenae. A few Linear B tablets and inscribed jars show palace administration. Greek myth tied it to Perseus and to Heracles, who served King Eurystheus.
kingdom-of-tiryns.e: The palace was destroyed c. 1200 BCE, but unlike most centres Tiryns continued, with a large lower town and a rebuilt hall into the 12th century BCE. It later became a small city absorbed by Argos c. 470 BCE. Its walls are a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with Mycenae.

kingdom-of-deira.t: The Anglian kingdom of the Yorkshire Wolds and York, whose boys in a Roman slave market are said to have inspired Pope Gregory's mission to the English.
kingdom-of-deira.o: Deira developed from Anglian settlement in east Yorkshire, perhaps taking over a British territory whose name it kept. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle names Aelle as its first king from 560. Bede tells how Gregory the Great, seeing Deiran slave boys in Rome, punned that they were not Angles but angels.
kingdom-of-deira.r: Deira's centre lay around York and the Wolds. Edwin, son of Aelle, ruled all Northumbria from 616, accepted baptism from Paulinus at York in 627 and built the first church on the site of York Minster. After his death in 633 Deira had its own kings again, including Oswine, killed on the orders of Oswiu in 651.
kingdom-of-deira.e: Bernician kings repeatedly dominated Deira. Its last sub-king, Oethelwald, supported Penda against Oswiu and disappeared after the Winwaed in 655. Deira became the southern half of the Kingdom of Northumbria, its name surviving in later sources.

kingdom-of-atholl.t: A Pictish kingdom in the central Highlands whose name, 'New Ireland', hints at Gaelic influence, later a Scottish earldom.
kingdom-of-atholl.o: Atholl, Athfotla, appears in Irish annals from the 8th century, when a king of Atholl was drowned by Oengus son of Fergus, king of the Picts, in 739. The name is usually interpreted as 'New Ireland', suggesting Gaelic settlement or influence in the Pictish highlands of Perthshire. Fotla is also one of the seven Pictish provinces.
kingdom-of-atholl.r: Atholl seems to have had its own kings within the Pictish overkingship. Its lands in the valleys of the Tay, Tummel and Garry were pastoral and thinly peopled. Dunkeld, on its edge, became a major church centre in the 9th century.
kingdom-of-atholl.e: Atholl was absorbed into the Kingdom of Scotland as a mormaerdom and later an earldom. Its rulers produced Crinan, abbot of Dunkeld, father of King Duncan I, linking Atholl with the royal house.

kingdom-of-seisyllwg.t: A Welsh kingdom of Ceredigion and Ystrad Tywi, named after King Seisyll, which merged with Dyfed to form Deheubarth.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.o: Seisyllwg was created when Seisyll ap Clydog of Ceredigion added Ystrad Tywi, the Tywi valley, to his realm in the 8th century. The new territory was named after him. Little else is known of its early rulers beyond genealogies.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.r: The kingdom covered much of later Cardiganshire and Carmarthenshire, a land of upland pasture and coastal farms with important churches such as Llanbadarn Fawr. Its last native king, Gwgon, drowned in 871, and it passed by marriage to Rhodri the Great of Gwynedd, whose son Cadell inherited it.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.e: Cadell's son Hywel Dda united Seisyllwg with Dyfed around 920, creating the Kingdom of Deheubarth. The name Seisyllwg fell out of use, though Ceredigion persists as a county.

kingdom-of-morgannwg.t: A south-east Welsh kingdom formed by the union of Glywysing and Gwent, whose name survives in Glamorgan.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.o: Morgannwg, 'Morgan's land', is traditionally named after Morgan Hen ab Owain, who united the older kingdoms of Glywysing and Gwent around 942. Earlier rulers of the region are known from the charters of the Book of Llandaff.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.r: The kingdom covered the fertile vale and uplands between the Tywi and the Wye, with churches such as Llandaff and Llancarfan. Its kings dealt with English rulers, and Morgan Hen attended Aethelstan's court. After his death in 974 Gwent and Glywysing separated again at times, and the kingdom was later ruled by Gruffydd ap Llywelyn and then Caradog ap Gruffydd.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.e: Iestyn ap Gwrgant, the last native ruler, was overthrown around 1090 by the Norman Robert Fitzhamon, who created the Lordship of Glamorgan. The name survives in the counties of Glamorgan.

kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.t: A small Anglian sub-kingdom on the Welsh border in Herefordshire and Shropshire, ruled by Merewalh's dynasty under Mercia.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.o: The Magonsaete, perhaps named after Magnis (Kenchester), emerged in the mid 7th century in the borderlands west of the Severn. Their first known ruler was Merewalh, whom later tradition made a son of Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia, though this is uncertain.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.r: Merewalh's family was noted for piety: his daughter Mildburh founded the abbey of Much Wenlock, and other children became saints. A bishopric at Hereford served the people. The rulers were sub-kings under Mercian overlordship, and the population included many Britons.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.e: The dynasty disappears from record in the 8th century, and the territory was absorbed directly into Mercia. Its outline survived as the diocese of Hereford.

kingdom-of-limerick.t: A Norse town-kingdom on the Shannon estuary whose fall to the Dal Cais opened the way for Brian Boru's rise.
kingdom-of-limerick.o: Vikings had raided the Shannon since the 9th century, and in 922 Tomrair mac Ailchi established a permanent fleet base at Limerick, Hlymrekr. The settlement competed with the Kingdom of Dublin for control of the Irish Sea trade and raided deep into Connacht and Munster.
kingdom-of-limerick.r: Limerick was a fortified trading port on an island in the Shannon, dealing in slaves and plunder. Its kings were rivals of Dublin's dynasty, losing a war with them in 937. In the 960s Ivar of Limerick allied with Irish kings of Munster against the rising Dal Cais.
kingdom-of-limerick.e: Mathgamain and Brian Boru of the Dal Cais defeated the Norse at Sulcoit in 967 and sacked the town. Brian killed Ivar and his sons on Scattery Island in 977. Limerick became the O'Brien capital and later the seat of the Kingdom of Thomond.

kingdom-of-epirus.t: Kingdom of the Molossians in north-west Greece, whose Aeacid kings led the Epirote peoples and produced Pyrrhus, Rome's most famous Greek opponent.
kingdom-of-epirus.o: The Molossian kings claimed descent from Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, and were called Aeacids. Their kingdom in the mountains of Epirus emerges into history in the 5th century BCE; King Tharyps, educated at Athens, introduced Greek institutions and letters. The Molossians gradually led the other Epirote tribes, the Chaonians and Thesprotians, in an alliance.
kingdom-of-epirus.r: Kings ruled alongside an assembly and annual magistrates, swearing to govern by law. The economy rested on pastoralism, with Dodona's oracle of Zeus as the great religious centre. Alexander I, brother of Olympias and uncle of Alexander the Great, campaigned in southern Italy until his death in 331 BCE. Pyrrhus (297-272 BCE) made Ambracia his capital and won costly victories over Rome.
kingdom-of-epirus.e: After Pyrrhus died at Argos in 272 BCE, his successors struggled against Macedon and the Aetolians. The last of the royal line, Deidamia, was killed around 232 BCE and the monarchy was replaced by the Epirote League. Pyrrhus survives in the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'.

kingdom-of-castile.t: The medieval kingdom of Castile, which took Toledo, crushed the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa and became the dominant power of Christian Iberia.
kingdom-of-castile.o: The County of Castile had been raised to a kingdom by Ferdinand I, who also ruled the Kingdom of León. At his death in 1065 he divided his realms, leaving Castile to his eldest son Sancho II. After Sancho's murder in 1072 his brother Alfonso VI reunited Castile and León.
kingdom-of-castile.r: Castile was a frontier society of free settlers, town councils with their own fueros and mounted warriors, later organised in military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago. Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085. Alfonso VIII, defeated at Alarcos in 1195, led the coalition that destroyed the Almohad army at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Burgos, on the pilgrim road to Santiago, prospered on trade and wool.
kingdom-of-castile.e: Castile and León were separated again from 1157, but in 1230 Ferdinand III, already king of Castile, inherited León, creating the lasting union known as the Crown of Castile, which absorbed most of al-Andalus within a generation.

kingdom-of-deheubarth.t: The kingdom of south-west Wales, founded by Hywel Dda and later led by the Lord Rhys, a centre of Welsh law, poetry and resistance to Norman conquest.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.o: Deheubarth, 'the southern part', was formed around 920 when Hywel Dda united his inheritance of the Kingdom of Seisyllwg with Dyfed. Hywel later also ruled Gwynedd and Powys, and became the only Welsh king to issue coins.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.r: Hywel was credited with codifying Welsh law, the Cyfraith Hywel, which governed inheritance, compensation and status. The kingdom's centre was Dinefwr in the Tywi valley. Norman lords overran much of it after 1093, but Rhys ap Gruffydd, the Lord Rhys, rebuilt its power, held the first recorded eisteddfod at Cardigan in 1176 and patronised Strata Florida Abbey.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.e: After the Lord Rhys died in 1197, his sons divided Deheubarth in bitter feuds. Its remnants came under Gwynedd's Principality of Wales, and its lands were absorbed by the English crown after 1283.

kingdom-of-moray.t: A powerful northern Scottish realm whose rulers, styled kings or mormaers, contested the Scottish throne, most famously through Macbeth.
kingdom-of-moray.o: Moray emerged in the 10th century in the lands around the Moray Firth after the decline of the Pictish kingdom of Fortriu. Its ruling family, probably from Cenel Loairn by later genealogies, sometimes appear in Irish annals as kings of Alba, reflecting their claims to the Kingdom of Scotland.
kingdom-of-moray.r: Moray's rulers commanded a rich coastal plain and highland hinterland. Macbeth, mormaer of Moray, killed Duncan I in 1040 and ruled Scotland until 1057, making a pilgrimage to Rome. His stepson Lulach briefly succeeded him. The house of Moray clashed repeatedly with Norse earls of Orkney and with the line of Malcolm III.
kingdom-of-moray.e: After Angus of Moray died in battle at Stracathro in 1130, David I annexed the province, planting burghs and Flemish settlers. Revolts by MacWilliam claimants continued into the 13th century.
